articles.title: Lord's digs up cricket pitch - why the drastic action and what next?
articles.summary: After years of comment, Lord's has dug up one of its pitches for the first time in more than 25 years. Why the drastic action and what next?
articles.body:
It is the sight no-one has seen for a generation.

Diggers in front of Lord's famous old pavilion. A gaping hole in the middle of the square.

After years of issues and complaints around the playing surface at cricket's spiritual home, those in charge have taken the drastic step to dig up one of its strips.

So what caused it, what is being done and what does it mean for the future?

Lord's has 20 across the square but nine is one of five central strips used for the most high-profile matches.

Crucially, it was the controversial surface used for England's Test against New Zealand in June - a surface that proved incredibly difficult for batting.

Jacob Bethell was bowled by a ball that shot along the ground and the Test would have been over inside two days had it not been for bad weather.

Afterwards, England captain Ben Stokes said the surface does not benefit Test cricket and it was rated as "unsatisfactory" by the International Cricket Council.

Cricket's most historic venue had to deal with the ignominy of a demerit point being placed on its record.

The New Zealand Test was not the first case of Lord's - which is effectively guaranteed at least two Tests per year by the England and Wales Cricket Board - having trouble with its playing surface.

The pitches used for the men's Tests against Ireland in 2019, New Zealand in 2021 and Australia in 2023, plus a women's one-day international against India in 2022, were all rated "average" under the ICC's previous system.

Lord's has often been criticised for being slow and low, thus providing less entertaining cricket.

Back in February, the MCC stated the "square must be at the forefront of the club's priorities" and in the summer it set out a seven-point "pitch action plan", which has included bringing in external experts.

As reported by Cricinfo , external , this month things have gone a step further.

Over five days, Pitch Nine was dug up and the 22-yard hole filled with a base layer of gravel.

The area has been rolled and tended to by the groundstaff and fresh soil was added on top. It now looks little different to the square around it.

In a letter sent to members last week, the MCC chair Mark Nicholas warned "we should all be braced for the scheduling challenges" their pitch plans will bring.

Pitch Nine will be out of action until 2029 at the earliest, depriving Lord's of one of its main TV pitches.

Major matches next year include the second men's Ashes Test in late June, a women's Ashes one-day international in July, a men's Test against Bangladesh in May, and a men's ODI in September.

Lord's plans to cope as best it can and the MCC has also stepped up its plans around hybrid pitches.

Lord's already has two hybrids, where synthetic fibres are inserted and mixed with a regular grass pitch, and a third will be added to the square in the spring.

Hybrids are not currently allowed in Test cricket but are allowed in white-ball internationals and domestic cricket.

They can be revitalised and reused more quickly than natural surfaces, which could relieve some of the pressure caused by the loss of Pitch Nine.

And Lord's is also continuing with its plans to introduce drop-in surfaces.

Drop-ins - pitches which are grown away from the main square before being 'dropped' into place - are common in Australia and New Zealand but not in the UK.

After Nicholas said earlier this year drop-ins could be used as early as 2028, the first trays will be introduced to the Nursery Ground in the coming weeks.

"The work now underway represents the most comprehensive review of the square and pitch preparation at Lord's in a generation," Nicholas told members.

"While these changes will take time to deliver their full benefit, they will help to ensure that the club prepares pitches worthy of the ground's reputation."

Time will tell whether the changes are as successful as hoped.

articles.title: South Africa v Australia: Tourists bundled out for 99 in stark collapse
articles.summary: Australia are forced to follow-on for only the third time in the past 38 years after being dismissed for 99 by South Africa on day four of the second Test in Gqeberha.
articles.body:
Second Test, Gqeberha (day four of five)

South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81

Australia were forced to follow-on for only the third time in the past 38 years after being dismissed for 99 by South Africa on day four of the second Test in Gqeberha.

Left-armer Marco Jansen took a superb 5-33 and Kagiso Rabada and Wiaan Mulder two wickets each as the Proteas roared back into the Test to give them a real shot at leveling the series.

They were 110-6 early on day three, their hopes severely dented, but scrapped to 425-9 after Temba Bavuma's 179 and now take a 326-run first innings lead.

After opener Nic Maddinson was dismissed late on day three, South Africa took the remaining nine wickets inside 40 overs on the fourth day.

Steve Smith was the tourists highest scoring with 28. No other batter passed 14 and the highest partnership was just 23.

The last time Australia were forced to follow-on was against India at Sydney in 2019. Before that, the most recent previous occasion was the fourth Ashes Test at Trent Bridge in 2005.

It was also the biggest first-innings deficit they conceded since a Test against West Indies in November 1984.

Jansen sparked the collapse by nicking off nightwatchman Scott Boland with his first ball of the day at the start of the second over.

Four overs later he pinned Travis Head lbw on review for 14 and Marnus Labuschagne was brilliantly caught at slip by Simon Harmer off the bowling of Anrich Nortje for the same score.

Nortje was only able to bowl 3.3 overs because of an apparent groin issue, which will impact the remainder of the Test if he is unable to bowl again.

After Jansen found the edge of Matt Renshaw and Alex Carey in the same over, he also had Beau Webster caught in similar fashion for his fifth Test five-wicket haul.

Mitchell Starc and Australia captain Pat Cummins followed within 11 balls of Mulder bowling Smith, who had been given treatment to his neck throughout his 88 balls, and, after a brief conversation with his bowlers, captain Bavuma signaled to Australia's dressing room that they would have to bat again.

South Africa now have more than 150 overs to complete victory.

articles.title: Ranji Trophy: Railways spoil Rajasthan’s victory push with gritty draw
articles.summary: JAIPUR: Echoing the outcome of their opening fixture against Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan once again settled for three points as their Ranji Trophy Group ‘D’
articles.body: JAIPUR: Echoing the outcome of their opening fixture against Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan once again settled for three points as their Ranji Trophy Group ‘D’ match against Railways ended in a draw at the Sawai Man Singh Stadium here on Wednesday, securing the advantage courtesy of a first-innings lead. Rajasthan's hopes of pressing for an outright victory were hampered by injuries to key bowlers. Pacer Akash Singh hurt his right hand while completing a caught-and-bowled dismissal of Mohammad Saif in the first innings, while left-arm spinner Ajay Kukna developed finger swelling, leaving him unable to bowl at full capacity.Resuming the final morning at 305/6, Railways folded within the first hour to finish their first innings at 338. Kukna emerged as the standout bowler with figures of 4 for 106, a stellar spell that earned him appreciation even from the opposition camp.Acknowledging his threat, Railways centurion Saif, who struck 103 not out off 118 balls (8x4, 4x6), said, “This pitch wasn’t really an outright result wicket and no bowler was that difficult to play. But I would specially praise Kukna, because taking five wickets in the last match and four wickets here is no easy feat. He puts a good loop on the ball.”Having restricted the visitors, Rajasthan enforced the follow-on. Railways quickly lost both openers when they came out to bat again in a hectic first session that saw six wickets tumble across the morning action, the only window where the bowlers extracted life from the surface. However, that early flurry proved to be the last twist in the tale.Any hopes Rajasthan harboured of forcing an outright victory on the placid track were firmly dashed by a third-wicket partnership of unbeaten 155, compounded further by the team's young and inexperienced bowling attack.Rajasthan captain Kartik Sharma acknowledged the team’s inability to extract wickets. “The plan was to get them out quickly and enforce the follow-on, and that's exactly what happened. But later on, wickets stopped coming. Plus, our bowlers Akash and Kukna got injured. Hopefully, Kukna will recover by the next match and we will know about Akash's status soon,” he added.Eshaan Goyal and Saif dug their heels in, frustrating the hosts through the remainder of the day. Goyal provided a watchful anchor with an undefeated 59 off 132 deliveries.With the surface giving bowlers virtually no room to maneuver, the match meandered to a tame draw as Railways safely reached 176/2 in their second innings when stumps were drawn.The Rajasthan captain backed his young pace attack, saying, “First of all, our bowling attack is not weak. And, we have to introduce young players into the side eventually, so we are looking ahead and building them. They need to be prepared and gain experience, and this is the exact time for our young bowlers to gain that exposure,” he explained.Rajasthan will next take on Uttarakhand in Dehradun from October 26.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Jalaj Saxena equals Bishan Singh Bedi as Kerala notch up innings win against Odisha in Ranji Trophy
articles.summary: The ball gripped, the bails flew, and rain threatened to play party-pooper. But Kerala found its voice under the dark, sombre clouds.
articles.body: The ball gripped, the bails flew, and rain threatened to play party-pooper. But Kerala found its voice under the dark, sombre clouds. By the time the final Odisha wicket tumbled at the Greenfield Stadium in Thiruvananthapuram on Wednesday afternoon, the hosts had notched up an innings win with seven vital points on their home turf. Kerala needed a little over 23 overs to wrap up Odisha’s innings for 143 and register an innings and 36-run win.At the centre was Jalaj Saxena, the veteran off-spinner, who mesmerised Odisha with his bagful of tricks to finish with figures of 5/34 from 18 overs.This was Jalaj’s 35th five-wicket haul in the Ranji Trophy, a phenomenal number that puts him level with the great Bishan Singh Bedi for the joint fifth-most five-fors in the tournament’s history. Odisha, meanwhile, became the 20th Ranji team he has taken five wickets against.Quiz him on his record-breaking day, though, and the man shrugs. “I didn’t know about equalling Bishan paaji,” he says. “Who is the bowler with the highest five-fors? Is it Rajinder Goel?” he asks. Jalaj is correct.The legendary slow-left-arm orthodox spinner holds the record for the most five-wicket hauls in the Ranji Trophy, with 59 five-fors.The recipe for Jalaj’s success is built on his love for the game. “I just love the feeling of putting on the whites and playing for four days,” Jalaj tells TOI.In the offseason, he worked tirelessly on his fitness, assiduously strengthening his back and core to build stamina for bowling longer spells.“Odisha was already on the backfoot and were four wickets down coming into the final day. The plan was simple: land the ball in the right areas,” he explains.Jalaj landed the ball in the right areas, and the pitch did the rest. Like a true team man, Jalaj credits the group and not himself for this resounding win. “It is a team effort,” he says.The platform was set by Kerala’s batters, with centuries from Sachin Baby and Mohammed Azharuddeen.At 39, the age when most cricketers walk into the sunset, Jalaj is hungry and still looks to climb the ladder. “If you don’t have long-term goals, then there is no point in playing Ranji Trophy,” he quips. “Progressing to the next level is what I always aspire to,” he elaborates.“If you ask Sachin and Azhar, even they have aspirations of playing in the IPL and representing India,” Jalaj explains.His never-say-die attitude could rub off on some of Kerala’s younger players. Among them is off-spinner Vaisakh Chandran, who made a comeback to first-class cricket in the previous game against Jharkhand.“I love bowling in tandem with Vaisakh. He is a talented off-spinner and a keen learner,” he adds.The timing makes this win sweeter. With the festival in the air, Saxena has delivered the perfect Dussehra gift for Kerala. Next up is Bengal. “Taking it one game at a time. Not looking too far ahead,” Jalaj concludes.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: James Anderson not offered new contract by Lancashire
articles.summary: James Anderson’s legendary career could be over after Lancashire opt against offering England’s all-time leading wicket-taker a new deal.
articles.body:
James Anderson's legendary career could be over after Lancashire opted against offering England's all-time leading wicket-taker a new contract.

Anderson, 44, chose to continue playing with Lancashire after England forced him into international retirement in 2024.

He captained Lancashire in the County Championship last season but the Red Rose endured a poor campaign, finishing next to bottom of Division Two.

Now, as first reported by the Times, Anderson will not be given the opportunity to play at Old Trafford in 2027 - the summer when he will turn 45.

It is not known whether Anderson will retire or look to extend his 26-year professional career with another county.

Anderson first played top-level cricket as a 17-year-old for Lancashire Cricket Board in 2000, then made his Lancashire debut the following year.

His exit from the Red Rose comes at a time of upheaval at Old Trafford. The county are undergoing a review of their cricket operations, led by interim chair Dame Sarah Storey and new chief executive Richard Kenyon. Paul Farbrace was appointed as Lancashire's director of cricket earlier this month.

Although Anderson is in his mid-40s, he has remained in supreme form in a struggling team.

He took 50 wickets in the County Championship in 2026, a tally bettered by only six other bowlers in Division Two. Anderson was named Lancashire's Championship player of the year.

Overall, 443 of Anderson's 1,193 first-class wickets came for Lancashire, to go with 83 List A wickets and 50 T20 wickets for the county.

In a 23-year international career, Anderson took 991 wickets across formats for England. Only spinners Muttiah Muralitharan of Sri Lanka and Australia's Shane Warne have more in international cricket.

In 2024, Anderson became the third bowler in Test history, after Muralitharan and Warne, to reach 700 wickets. He remains third on the all-time list with 704, a record for a pace bowler that is unlikely to be broken.

Later that year, Anderson was asked to call time on his international career by England's then hierarchy of coach Brendon McCullum, captain Ben Stokes and director of cricket Rob Key.

He played his 188th and final Test against West Indies at Lord's before embarking on a short spell as England's bowling consultant.

In 2025, Anderson signed a new deal with Lancashire and suggested he could play county cricket for three more seasons. In April of that year, he was knighted for services to cricket.

Anderson stood in as Lancashire captain during the 2025 season and was given the job full-time for 2026.

He was understood to be enjoying the role and, at the end of the this summer, there was no suggestion Anderson would end his career.

On Wednesday, as reports of his exit from Old Trafford began to emerge, those close to Anderson were unaware of the situation. Lancashire have not commented.

articles.body: India, led by Shreyas Iyer, will look to extend their unbeaten run in T20I series in New Zealand as they begin a five-match rubber against the hosts on Thursday. The visitors, despite having limited time to rest, acclimatise and train after their arrival, will rely on their batting strength to take on the home side.India's most recent T20I series in New Zealand was in 2022. India went on to win the series, claiming victory in the only match that was not affected by rain.Only four batters in India's squad have played T20Is in New Zealand before — captain Iyer, Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson and Shivam Dube. While Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma and 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi bring plenty of attacking options, they will need time to adjust to the pace and seam movement expected in local conditions.For Iyer, the series is an opportunity to prove himself on an overseas tour after his tenure as captain began with consecutive defeats in Ireland and England.Mitchell Santner's New Zealand side will look to put India under pressure. Iyer arrives after leading India to their second consecutive gold-winning campaign at the Asian Games and a hard-fought home series against the West Indies that ended in a draw.However, if the series follows the pattern of India's tour of the UK earlier this year, scrutiny of Iyer's leadership is likely to increase. He is expected to lead India at the T20 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand in two years.India will be without two key players in all-rounder Hardik Pandya, who is injured, and pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah, who will feature only in the ODI and Test legs of the tour. articles.body:
England's highest Test wicket-taker and the most prolific fast bowler in the history of the game took 704 wickets in 188 matches before his final appearance against the West Indies in 2024.

The 44-year-old had a strong season captaining his county in 2026, taking 50 wickets at an average of 17 amid Lancashire's struggles in Division Two of the County Championship.

However, the Red Rose county have opted against offering him a new deal for the 2027 season.

Across his career, Anderson has taken 1,193 first-class wickets at 24. Not only that, he claimed 358 dismissals in ODI cricket and 71 in T20s.

Anderson continued to play for Lancashire when England moved on from him in July 2024 and last year he took the captaincy of his boyhood club, where he has an end named after him at Old Trafford.

Lancashire finished second bottom of Division Two when they were strong favourites for promotion.

Lancashire have recently appointed Richard Kenyon as chief executive and Paul Farbrace as director of cricket to lead the rebuild, and Anderson is not a part of their plan.

As first reported by The Times , it is understood Anderson is set to end a long association with Lancashire that began 25 years ago, leaving his future up in the air.

articles.title: 'Everyone has shown the competence to beat everyone else': Gary Stead warns New Zealand against taking home advantage for granted
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Home advantage is losing its sheen in international cricket, with teams increasingly equipped to beat opponents in the latter's own backyard.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Home advantage is losing its sheen in international cricket, with teams increasingly equipped to beat opponents in the latter's own backyard. Former head coach Gary Stead believes hosts New Zealand may not enjoy the edge they once did when India begin their tour with the T20 series beginning on Thursday, with the visitors’ improved pace attack and the ability to adapt to challenging conditions making them a formidable opponent.The 54-year-old, who oversaw a successful phase in New Zealand cricket, including their World Test Championship triumph, said the days of exploiting an opponent’s perceived weakness were fading.“Earlier, you played India and thought, ‘Oh, we’ll do a green track because they don’t have good seamers.’ Now they have quality seamers as well,” Stead said.Referring to New Zealand’s 3-0 triumph in the 2024 Test series in India, he added: “The same way, when we came in 2024, we had quality spinners too. The whole idea of home advantage has disappeared a little bit around the world. Everyone has shown the competence to beat everyone else at any given time. So you’ve got to be on your game and be sharp.”Stead, currently head coach of Andhra’s Ranji Trophy team, believes India’s ability to adapt to New Zealand’s bouncy surfaces will be crucial to their chances.“The Indians are going to have to adapt to bouncy wickets, some of the bounciest possibly in the world. The wickets will have bounce and carry. If the Indian players can nullify New Zealand’s bowlers, then I think it’ll be a cracking series,” he said.The Test matches, in particular, could pose the toughest challenge. Stead pointed to Hagley Oval in Christchurch and Basin Reserve Wellington as venues traditionally known for their extra bounce.“It's very important for New Zealand. India are obviously an amazing Test side, and then we go to Australia and play, so there are six huge Tests coming up for New Zealand. But if you want to be judged against the best, you’ve got to compete against the best as well,” he said.With Australia and South Africa also producing compelling Test cricket recently, Stead believes the influence of T20 cricket is increasingly visible in the longest format.“I think the T20 format has allowed players a little bit more freedom in the way they play. And I think that’s rubbing off on Test cricket now as well,” he said.Stead also called on the International Cricket Council (ICC) to explore more multi-format series, arguing that longer tours could help sustain interest across formats.“Personally, I think the ICC should consider playing more multi-format series. Rather than teams coming and going very quickly and people forgetting about the series, it could be a little like the women’s Ashes, where they have multi-format scenarios. I really think it’s something that could take off,” he said.However, he acknowledged that fitting longer tours into an increasingly crowded international calendar would be difficult, with teams constantly preparing for the next World Cup in one of the two white-ball formats.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: England cricket: Brendon McCullum believes his relationship with Harry Brook has 'blossomed' over the past 18 months
articles.summary: As England engage in a rare tri-series tournament, white-ball head coach Brendon McCullum reflects on his time as Test coach and heaps praise on white-ball captain Harry Brook; watch England vs Sri Lanka live on Sky Sports Cricket from 8.30am (first ball 9am) Thursday
articles.body:
The New Zealander took charge of the Test side in 2022 and took control of all three formats in 2025. However, in July, a month after then captain Ben Stokes' dramatic international retirement, he stepped away from the Test game that had become such troublesome terrain.

"In a funny way, I think, sort of now, Harry and I, our relationship as the captain and coach over the last 18 months or so has really blossomed, and I think we work fantastically well together," McCullum told Sky Sports.

Brook has held the mantle of T20 and ODI captain since Jos Buttler stepped away from the role in April 2025.

Under his leadership, the T20 side is now ranked top of the global rankings and, despite a disappointing 87-run defeat by Pakistan in their opening match in Rawalpindi, the one-day side is slowly moving in the right direction.

McCullum reflects on 'eventful Bazball era

To succinctly summarise McCullum's tenure would be tricky, owing to the multitude of highs, lows and nightclub incidents - Brook himself making headlines after a hushed-up scuffle with a nightclub bouncer in Wellington last winter.

"Eventful is a good word, but in a funny old way I think things worked out really well," he said, before praising Brook's leadership and technical abilities.

"He's grown immensely as a leader in the last 12 months in particular.

"He's obviously a brilliant tactician, but he commands the respect of the dressing room as well."

When Test captain Ben Stokes retired in dramatic fashion a month prior to McCullum's eventual departure in July 2026, Brook was near the top of the small number of potential replacements.

Ultimately however, occupying the captaincy of all three formats was deemed too much responsibility for the Yorkshire batter and veteran Joe Root was once again called upon.

McCullum took the red ball helm in 2022, setting sail on the Bazball voyage alongside his appointed skipper Ben Stokes. This came after a bleak period of stagnation where England played 44 Tests between 2019 - 2022, winning 15 and losing 22.

"I think the last four years that I had in the Test job was something I'm immensely proud of," McCullum said.

"It's one of the highlights of the time that I've had in cricket to be able to be in the privileged position of coaching the Test side and we achieved some good things."

For a while this flamboyant and aggressive style of cricket did reap reward. Ten wins out of 11 games kickstarted the campaign, but 17 losses with a return of 16 wins followed.

As well as an emphatic 4-1 Ashes thrashing Down Under.

"We obviously left a little bit on the table as well, but I have zero regrets about the time and I'm certainly content with where it all sits now," said McCullum.

McCullum fixed on 'the process' of World Cup glory

England began their tri-series with a disappointing loss to Pakistan, which raised eyebrows. McCullum's side will look to bounce back over the course of these games in the subcontinent, starting against Sri Lanka on Thursday, live on Sky Sports.

"I guess when you talk, everyone wants to win, right? Ultimately, we're all incredibly driven and competitive, and that's the ultimate goal," McCullum said.

"For us, it's more you're trying to work through the process of things. How do you stay calm during the moments to be able to make good decisions to allow your talent to come out?

"If we're good enough, we give ourselves an opportunity to play in another final. That's got to be great preparation for what we're hitting as well in terms of the World Cup (in late 2027).

"The last three series we've played., we've found ourselves in must-win games. We just won all three.

"So it'd be good if we continue to just improve as a side, keep getting better, keep getting more familiar with what we're trying to achieve. Ultimately, it'd be great if we were able to gain the success of winning this series."
